summary: estimated fetal weight is what the Fetal weight percentile calculator works out, and it gets there from the gestational age, the abdominal circumference, the head circumference and the biparietal diameter. Think of it as a shortcut for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Fetal weight percentile calculator work?
sections.html:
The Fetal weight percentile calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports estimated fetal weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sex); then you type in the gestational age, the abdominal circumference, the head circumference and the biparietal diameter.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in weeks. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Fetal weight percentile calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Estimated fetal weight=the exponential of ((1 ÷ 100000) × (61 × abdominal circumference × biparietal diameter − 386 × abdominal circumference × femur length + 4240 × abdominal circumference + 17400 × femur length + 640 × head circumference + 135960) × the natural log of (10))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Open the page and it is already filled in. With the values it starts from — Sex set to Unknown, Gestational age = 3360 wks, Abdominal circumference = 15.4 mm and Head circumference = 18 mm — it reports Estimated fetal weight = 23.577 g.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Estimated fetal weight = 23.577 g should be roughly the size you expected from Sex set to Unknown and Gestational age = 3360 wks.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in grams, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Time, opening in weeks
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Mass, opening in grams

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Fetal weight percentile calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the gestational age, the abdominal circumference and the head circumference — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Fetal weight percentile calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns estimated fetal weight, derived from the gestational age, the abdominal circumference and the head circumference. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Fetal weight percentile calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the gestational age, the abdominal circumference, the head circumference and the biparietal diameter, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter gestational age in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Gestational age opens in weeks and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Estimated fetal weight = 23.577 g. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Fetal weight percentile calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
